There are hundreds of aspiring writers, actors, and studio executives packed into the room. They all paid $199 to sit in an uncomfortable folding chair in a hotel ballroom for three
grueling days to learn one terrifying reality. If you do not plant a specific urgent question in the audience's mind, immediately they leave.
They will literally stand up and walk out of the theater or they will flip the channel. The inciting incident is the precise moment the reader's core question gets planted.
Without it, there is literally no reason to turn to page two. Let's look at classic examples.
In Jaws, it's the opening shark attack. The question instantly becomes, "Will they stop this monster before he kills again?" In The Matrix, the inciting incident is Neo taking the red pill.
The question becomes, will he survive the reality of this illusion and fulfill his destiny?
But here is the massive, almost mind-bending trick that Pressfield reveals from his Hollywood days.
Embedded in the DNA of the inciting incident is the climax. They are inextricably linked. The beginning dictates the ending.
The trick the pros use to ensure this works is something that sounds totally counterintuitive. Start at the end.
They solve the story's climax first and then they work completely backward to the inciting incident to layer in the emotional If we look at the logic of storytelling, it makes perfect sense.
The inciting incident is a promise. The climax is the fulfillment of that promise.

If the climax of the story is Luke Skywalker using the Force to blow up the Death Star, then the inciting incident has to be him discovering the hidden message from Princess Leia and meeting Obi-Wan Kenobi, who introduces him to the Force.
The DNA of the finale, the force, the rebellion, the stakes is explicitly planted in the very first disruption of the hero's normal world.
I have to push back on this working backward idea. It sounds so incredibly mechanical and soulless.

Doesn't that just kill the organic discovery of writing? I'm thinking of authors like Stephen King, who famously despise outlining. King says he just puts characters in a situation and watches what they do.

your build in act two isn't actually a build. It's just rambling. You're wandering in the dark, hoping you bump into a satisfying conclusion.
Working backward isn't stifling. It is liberating. It guarantees that the promise you made to the reader in the inciting incident is actually paid off and paid off on theme.
It ensures you don't write a gripping murder mystery for 300 pages and then end it with a sudden sci-fi alien invasion.
